problem: Existing multi-agent semantic navigation (Co-NavGPT, MCoCo-Nav) relies on a centralized planner or a globally aggregated map and supports only single categorical goals, while multimodal/multi-object navigation (GOAT) is single-agent only.
motivation: Robot teams searching for multiple objects given as category, language or image goals need to work without a central coordinator or shared global state, since centralization creates single points of failure and scales poorly. Real deployments have only intermittent ad-hoc connectivity, so coordination must tolerate that.
key_idea: Extend the GOAT instance-aware semantic mapping pipeline to teams by having each robot exchange maps, goal status and intent pairwise when in range, and select frontiers with a distance-ratio weight that implicitly allocates tasks.
insight: Pairwise opportunistic communication is enough to match or beat centralized/shared-map baselines. The communication ablation (r_comm=0.1 m vs 5 m) raises SR 68.6→74.6 and SPL 28.9→38.2, with the larger effect on SPL because robots avoid re-exploring teammates' areas. Much of the absolute gain also comes from single-agent fixes to GOAT (log-odds maps, goal-region selection, raycast exploration, YOLO verification), which raise GOAT-Bench single-agent SR from 26.3 to 44.0.
method: Single-agent backbone: GOAT-style 2D top-down semantic map (obstacle/explored/navigable + semantic channels) with instance memory; goal matching by category lookup, CLIP for language, SuperGlue for images; frontier exploration.

Pairwise communication protocol: robots within 5 m range exchange semantic map, location, goal status and intent. Full map sends are limited by a per-neighbor cooldown τ (10 steps), with lightweight location/task messages in between.

Map alignment and merging: ORB matching on obstacle grid plus semantic landmark matching with a rotation-invariant radial descriptor, RANSAC for the rigid transform, validated by obstacle IoU and cached per neighbor. Log-odds maps are merged by taking the larger-magnitude value per cell to avoid double counting.
Intent broadcasting: robots remove goals that neighbors are pursuing; conflicts are resolved in favor of the higher-score robot, with ties broken by an initial unique priority.
Distance-weighted frontier selection: w(f,i)=min_{j in N(i)} d(f,p_j)/d(f,p_i) favors frontiers where robot i is closer than its neighbors, spreading the team without negotiation.
MSPL metric: MSPL=SR·d*/max{d*,max_j d_j}, where d* is the optimal makespan from a min-max multi-agent Generalized TSP MILP solved with Gurobi; reduces to SPL for one agent and one goal.

Single-agent improvements over GOAT: log-odds map accumulation, goal-region selection by dilation and clustering, raycast-based explored area, adaptive local planning, YOLOv10/YOLO-World detection verification, stair detection, score thresholding, segmentation refinement.

results: On HM3Dv0.2 with two agents, DM3-Nav gets SR 74.6 / SPL 38.2 (vs MCoCo-Nav 71.6/38.7 and Co-NavGPT 66.1/33.1), and 89.9/52.8 with GT semantics, beating both on all metrics. On GOAT-Bench multi-object, four robots reach SR 34.5 vs 24.6 for one robot under a 200-step budget, and the single-agent implementation improves on GOAT (SR 44.0 vs 26.3).
limitations: MSPL falls as team size grows (0.42 with 1 robot to 0.35 with 4), showing that redundant exploration under intermittent communication is not fully resolved.
Uses a simple distance-ratio heuristic and unlimited-quality ideal proximity communication (5 m range); real-world validation is a single qualitative office run with two robots.
Compute-heavy perception stack (Detic, YOLO-World, CLIP, SuperGlue); SPL is slightly below MCoCo-Nav on HM3Dv0.2 with predicted semantics (38.2 vs 38.7).
